definition: Baroque means extravagantly ornate and elaborate — worked over layer upon layer, past all restraint.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word baroque. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know baroque should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The palace chapel is baroque to the last inch: not a hand's width of wall is left plain beneath the carved angels, the twisting marble garlands, and the gold.
Fancy is much milder than baroque — a ribbon here, a flourish there, decoration that still knows when to stop.
Rococo goes further than baroque: the ornament multiplies and turns playful until the structure underneath all but disappears.

Ornate is rich decoration sitting on the surface of a thing — a carved frame, gilded covers, embroidered cuffs. Baroque goes further and deeper: the elaboration takes over the whole design, and the word stretches past objects to plans, rules, and prose.

Extravagant measures excess of any kind, especially spending — an extravagant gift can be one enormous diamond on a plain band. Baroque names a particular shape of excess: layer upon layer of worked detail, curling over every surface.

Portuguese barroco built nothing else in English — baroque arrived alone and stayed that way. Even rococo, the style-word most often spoken in the same breath, grows from a different root entirely (French rocaille, the pebble-and-shell garden work): neighbors in the showroom, not in the family tree.
Baroque means extravagantly ornate and elaborate — worked over layer upon layer, past all restraint.
The organ recital closed with a baroque toccata whose every phrase blossomed into runs and trills; by the third minute the melody was somewhere underneath, carrying more ornament than it could bear.
Baroque works on both of the word's registers at once.

Literally, the toccata belongs to the Baroque, the seventeenth-century style built on elaboration; critically, the performance is baroque because the ornament has swallowed what it was meant to decorate — the melody survives somewhere under the trills, but only just.
When the elaboration takes over the thing itself, the word applies.
critical when lowercase, neutral as the period name
Capitalized, Baroque names the seventeenth-century period — Bach's Baroque concertos are a classification, not a complaint.
Lowercase, it is a verdict: extravagantly over-elaborated.
And it is this unit's word for structure rather than surface — a contract, a bureaucracy, or an excuse can be baroque.
Beside its unit-mates: florid describes overworked language and garish loud color, while baroque says the whole design has vanished under its own elaboration.

baroque: Rococo goes further than baroque: the ornament multiplies and turns playful until the structure underneath all but disappears.
When the city reopened its nineteenth-century opera house, visitors expected gilding, and they got it.
But the restorers' notes reveal how far past simple gilding the building goes.
Every column sprouts carved vines; every vine hides trumpeting cherubs; the cherubs hold garlands that spill onto the next column.
The critic Elena Marsh calls the hall 'honestly baroque': ornament is not applied to the design — it is the design, worked into every surface until no plain inch remains.
Marsh contrasts it with the city hall across the square, where a single carved doorway decorates an otherwise sober facade.
There, she writes, decoration behaves itself.
In the opera house, it rules.
